justification: Formed a fresh judgement first, then checked the round-1 major against the new section. WebSearch for the query itself was already exhausted session-wide (same shared-budget situation round 1 hit), so I went straight to WebFetch on the pages that anchor the top results for 'tcp vs udp': GeeksforGeeks' TCP-vs-UDP comparison (a template comparison table, moderate depth, no code, no RFC citations, and 'flow control and congestion control' appears only as an unglossed table cell -- exactly the gap this article had in round 1) and Wikipedia's TCP article (deeper, has a real congestion-control section naming 'slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, and fast recovery' and distinguishing congestion control from the receive window, but with no runnable code, no measured numbers, and no verbatim RFC text). Verification performed: ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/networking/tcp-vs-udp.md` myself from PowerShell -- PASS, 17 blocks/8 executed, matching round 1. Diffed the round-2 writer commit (b55a054) against round 1's content to see the actual change: a new 'Congestion control: TCP's other brake' section plus RFC 5681 added to front-matter sources, a toolchain-statement move to comply with the editorial brief's 'state it once, where measurements appear' rule, and a genuine accuracy fix in the payment exercise (dropped an unsupported 'exactly once' claim about TCP and replaced it with the correct, hedged idempotency-key point) -- a voluntary improvement beyond what round 1 asked for. For the new section itself, I re-fetched RFC 5681 sections 2, 3 and 3.1 myself, plus RFC 9293 section 2, rather than trusting the article: 'a TCP increments cwnd by at most SMSS bytes for each ACK received that cumulatively acknowledges new data' (section 3.1) is verbatim; 'cwnd is incremented by roughly 1 full-sized segment per round-trip time' (section 3.1) is verbatim; 'the algorithms specified in this document work in terms of using loss as the signal of congestion' (section 3) is verbatim; 'implementing congestion control (e.g., [RFC 5681]) is a TCP requirement, but it is a complex topic on its own and not described in detail in this document' is verbatim from RFC 9293 section 2 and correctly attributes the RFC 5681 pointer. The article's own claim that 'a connection may only have the smaller of [cwnd and rwnd] in flight at once' is also verbatim-supported by RFC 5681 section 2's definition of cwnd ('a TCP MUST NOT send data with a sequence number higher than the sum of the highest acknowledged sequence number and the minimum of cwnd and rwnd'), which the article does not quote but states correctly. The slow-start-roughly-doubles-per-RTT framing and the congestion-avoidance linear-growth framing are both standard, accurate readings of RFC 5681 3.1, and the section is honest about why no loopback program on the page can show cwnd moving (no queued/shared link, so the only signal congestion control reacts to, loss, never occurs) rather than faking a demo. This fully and accurately resolves round 1's major finding, so the article no longer conflates flow control and congestion control or leaves the concept unglossed and uncited. What keeps it at 8.5 rather than higher: the new section frames loss detection as happening only 'the same way the retransmission timeout earlier detects one,' which is true but incomplete -- RFC 5681 section 3.2 gives fast retransmit (three duplicate ACKs) as the mechanism that actually catches most real-world loss, with a materially different response (fast recovery, not a full reset to slow start) than an RTO-driven cut; the section never names it, so a reader comes away thinking RTO is the only loss signal congestion control acts on. Both minor issues from round 1 remain open and unaddressed in this pass: the length-prefix framing helpers still use `BitConverter` with no note that the demo works only because both loopback ends share endianness, and the 'Change the size of the slack' exercise's measured '64 of 200' result still lives in a plain ```text block outside any `run-code.mjs`-checked fence. None of these three items is a factual error (nothing stated is false, only incomplete), and code still passes end to end, so neither the factual-error cap nor the failing-code cap applies. Against the compared pages, this article is now clearly more rigorous than GeeksforGeeks in every dimension and matches or exceeds Wikipedia's TCP article on citation discipline and hands-on verification while still trailing it narrowly on completeness (no fast retransmit/fast recovery) -- that combination is the 8.5, MDN/Real-Python-with-nits anchor, not higher.

issues.location: "Congestion control: TCP's other brake" section, final sentence of the third paragraph ("A dropped segment, detected the same way the retransmission timeout earlier detects one, tells the sender it pushed too hard, and `cwnd` is cut back, not merely paused.")
issues.problem: This states congestion-control loss detection happens only via the retransmission timeout, the mechanism the article already covered for basic reliability. RFC 5681 section 3.2 defines fast retransmit, triggered by three duplicate ACKs, as a second, faster loss-detection path that in practice catches most losses before an RTO would fire, and it leads to fast recovery (cwnd set to roughly ssthresh, not reset to one segment) rather than the slow-start restart an RTO-driven loss causes. As written, a reader has no reason to think TCP has any loss-detection path for congestion control other than the timer, which understates how TCP actually behaves on a lossy network and leaves an algorithm RFC 5681 names (per the editorial brief's own rule that every named algorithm gets its cost and conditions) uncovered.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add one or two sentences naming fast retransmit: duplicate ACKs (RFC 5681 section 3.2, "the fast retransmit algorithm uses the arrival of 3 duplicate ACKs ... as an indication that a segment has been lost") let a sender detect and resend a lost segment without waiting for the RTO, and the resulting cwnd cut (fast recovery) is gentler than an RTO-triggered reset to slow start. A code demo is not required, the same way none was required for the RTO-based mechanism on loopback.

issues.problem: The length-prefix header still uses `BitConverter`'s platform byte order (little-endian on x64) with no note that this only works because client and server share a machine and architecture in this loopback demo. The article calls this scheme representative of what real wire protocols do; a real cross-machine implementation has to fix the byte order explicitly or two different-endian peers disagree on the header's meaning.
